extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students (those dealing with remedies/accounting in patent infringement suits)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for measuring, apportioning, and awarding a defendant's profits in patent-infringement cases, including allowable cost deductions, methods of apportionment, burden-of-proof rules, standards of comparison for 'use' infringements, and special rules for design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery of entire profits where mingled and inseparable
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a defendant mingled profits made as an infringer with those made otherwise, and there is no criterion by which they can be separated, the plaintiff is entitled to recover the whole profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle illustrated by cases where defendant's product contained the entire invention plus additions whose contribution to profit was not ascertainable; when separation is impossible the infringer must submit to recovery of the whole. Emphasis on inability to separate as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary structure rule (entire profits when claim covers unitary structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim infringed covers a unitary structure which is made and sold by the defendant without addition or change, the plaintiff is entitled to recover the entire profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important modification: if the real invention lies in a single element (an improvement) and the defendant's unitary article includes many non-infringing elements that can be apportioned, full profits may not be recoverable. Rule informed by Patent Office practice requiring a claim to include a completely operative combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements allowable as cost deductions when ascertaining defendant's costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When taking an account of profits, the elements allowed to enter into the defendant's cost include: (1) market value of materials on hand at start and actual cost of subsequent materials purchased; (2) money paid to persons employed in making/selling the infringing articles (including officers/stockholders); (3) proper remuneration for the labor of the infringer in conducting the infringement; (4) interest on borrowed money (not on capital stock except in limited circumstances); (5) expenses of selling including advertising and commissions; (6) miscellaneous expenses equitably chargeable (not taxes/insurance unless plant devoted entirely to infringing business); (7) royalties paid on other patents used in the infringing structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inquiry must be based on direct evidence; cannot be based on costs to other parties. Examples and nuances: salaries paid in lieu of partnership profits may not be allowable; interest on capital stock allowed only to the extent apportionable to the infringing business; royalties on third-party patents are deductible as costs attributable to non-infringing parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden-of-proof rule for apportionment (Westinghouse principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff must first prove the existence of profits attributable to its invention and demonstrate that apportionment is impossible; if the plaintiff does this, the burden of separation shifts to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court statements: difficulty is not enough — must show impossibility or that defendant's conduct made apportionment impossible; plaintiff's evidence need only establish every element except the apportionment where defendant's books/employees show it cannot be done. If burden shifts, defendant must distinguish his own profits or lose them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a product contains additional ascertainable-value features, plaintiff recovers only attributable profits
rubrics_metrics.description: If the thing made and sold by the defendant contains other inventions or features of ascertainable cost and provable value, the complainant (except in design cases) can recover only that part of the defendant's profit which was due to the infringing parts or features; burden on complainant to prove amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically some exceptions shifted burden after defendant proved existence of added features affecting price; courts also treated patented third-party features differently from unpatented added features. If defendant refuses to produce books or acts in bad faith, burden may be thrown on defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of separation need not be mathematically exact; inferences allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: The complainant's evidence as to separation of profits need not be severely accurate and may be sufficient where it furnishes a foundation for just inferences rather than certain knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts accept reasonable inferences from the available evidence; plaintiff does not need impossible precision to show apportionment or impossibility of apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate-sales measurement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant made and sold the complainant's invention separately, as well as in connection with other inventions, the profit made on the separate sales is the measure of that part to be credited to the complainant's invention for joint sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is fairer than dividing gross profits by comparative cost of elements, because comparative cost is not necessarily the best evidence of comparative utility or profit margin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalties to other patentees as measure of non-infringing part
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant paid or contracted to pay other patentees a royalty for parts of the thing not covered by the complainant's patent, that royalty may be taken as the measure of the part of gross profits due to that non-infringing part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: this rule should not be applied where division can be made under the separate-sales rule; royalties may understate profits due to non-infringing parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire profits recoverable when patented part makes whole article useful
rubrics_metrics.description: If the thing made and sold would be useless for its special purpose without the part covered by the complainant's patent (or no other known article would serve), then all the profits derived from making and selling the entire thing are due to the patented part and are recoverable by the complainant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognizes situations where the patented element is the essential feature creating demand for the entire product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment by cost proportion when no other rule applies
rubrics_metrics.description: When profits due to infringing and non-infringing elements cannot be separated by any other rule, apportionment may be made by dividing aggregate profits in proportion to the respective cost of the different parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on presumption similar articles sell at a like percentage profit on cost; this method tends to favor defendants (monopolies can enhance prices), and was applied historically in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent special rule and knowledge requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Special statute for design patents provides that total profits from manufacture/sale of articles to which the design (or a colorable imitation) has been applied shall be recoverable, but to recover under it the complainant must show the defendant knew of the complainant's design and patent, or at least facts putting him on inquiry for that patent, and knew the design was applied without license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In design cases the plaintiff must, if possible, apportion profits if entire profits are not due; knowledge/constructive knowledge is a prerequisite to recover total profits under statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits when infringement consists only in selling specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement consisted only in selling specimens of the patented article, profits are ascertained by deducting the cost of purchasing and selling the articles from the amount received for them when sold. If the patented part is part of a larger article with separate prices, gross profit on the patented thing is the difference of those prices, but must bear a proportionate share of selling expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If infringer bought and resold instead of making, similar rules apply with reasonable modifications; selling expenses of entire apparatus allocated proportionally to the patented part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting rule for 'use' infringements: standard-of-comparison method
rubrics_metrics.description: When unlawful using of a patented article or process constitutes the infringement, recoverable profits equal the advantage the defendant derived from using the complainant's invention over what he could have derived from using any other process or thing known prior to that invention (the 'standard of comparison').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advantage may be greater excellence, greater cheapness, or both, and may consist of affirmative gain or savings from loss. The standard must have been known prior to the invention but need not have been publicly available beyond what concerns the patent in suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage may be affirmative gain or savings; limitations on counting savings as profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage attributable to the patented method may be affirmative gain (producing valuable articles from otherwise useless materials) or savings from loss (reduced materials, labor, or fuel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Savings count as profits only insofar as they result in affirmative gains in the particular business where the invention was used; courts have sometimes refused to treat pure cost-avoidance savings as profits where no actual profit or business continuation would result without the patented method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of comparison need not have been used by defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of comparison that the defendant offers need not have been used by him at any time; evidence of its utility compared to the invention in suit may be drawn from others who used both under the same conditions or other convincing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant may show the standard was successfully used by others, and may receive credit for superior results obtained by third parties in applying the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff not required to prove absolute 'next best' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary for the complainant to prove that a particular process or thing was absolutely the next best at the time of infringement; plaintiff should select a proper standard of comparison and produce evidence of the advantage the defendant derived from using the complainant's invention over that selected standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring proof that no better alternative existed anywhere would be unreasonable and impossible; courts accept a reasonable selected comparator and evidence comparing advantage.
